**D1-P3238** · 3. Would this make building the semantic search easier?

**D1-P3239** · Yes, although I would describe it as building the semantic index, not training the model.

**D1-P3240** · The current multilingual-e5-small model is pretrained. The application uses it to generate embeddings for passages and queries. We are not training a new language model on the Livre du Ciel.

**D1-P3241** · Under the proposed approach:

**D1-P3242** · The editorial system produces one approved, continuous ENRICHI text.

**D1-P3243** · A single build process creates the source passages, their stable location mappings and the lexical search documents.

**D1-P3244** · Those passages are segmented and embedded for Par le sens.

**D1-P3245** · Reader, search and speaker-attribution checks all refer back to the same approved text and provenance map.

**D1-P3246** · The major benefit is eliminating disagreement about what text should be searched.

**D1-P3247** · It will not automatically solve relevance ranking, confidence calibration, model-loading delays or all semantic-search weaknesses. But it removes an unnecessary source of uncertainty before those questions arise.

**D1-P3248** · 4. What would we risk losing?

**D1-P3249** · There are three risks I would take particularly seriously.

**D1-P3250** · First, documentary integrity. ENRICHI is a composite editorial text, not necessarily a transcription of one historical edition. It should never be represented as an unmodified original. Distinct textual variants must remain identifiable.

**D1-P3251** · Second, existing user data. The current application uses stable paragraph and supplement identifiers, character offsets and source-mode information in reading positions, highlights, notes, collections and links. Flattening text without a verified migration map could damage them. This is probably the most serious technical migration risk.

**D1-P3252** · Third, release complexity. Combining an architectural refactoring with seven editorial corrections and a semantic-index rebuild would make any regression harder to diagnose.

**D1-P3253** · These risks are manageable, but they justify an incremental migration rather than directly rewriting v142.19.

**D1-P3290** · 1. Revised conclusion after examining the actual application

**D1-P3291** · I favour moving to one authoritative ENRICHI for the Reader and both search engines. But I would change an important part of my previous recommendation: we should simplify the published text and its technical pipeline without eliminating the underlying source distinctions.

**D1-P3292** · This is not merely a compromise. It is a different architecture that could remove the principal causes of the recent problems while retaining the evidence needed to establish that the text is correct.

**D1-P3293** · I have examined the frozen v142.19 application ZIP, including the actual Reader composition functions, supplement registry, lexical search engine, semantic runtime and semantic-pack manifest.

**D1-P3294** · Five findings materially affect the decision:

**D1-P3295** · Par le sens already has one ENRICHI semantic index. We would not be replacing three semantic models with one.

**D1-P3296** · The Reader still assembles supplementary passages dynamically. This creates additional complexity and can produce a reading different from the one represented in the semantic index.

**D1-P3297** · Par les mots, navigation, reading history and statistics depend on the selected documentary view. Eliminating those choices could simplify considerably more than the semantic engine itself.

**D1-P3298** · Existing highlights and reading positions are anchored to historical paragraph identities and text offsets. A careless merger could damage precisely the functionality we have spent considerable effort stabilising.

**D1-P3299** · Most of the long-term benefit can be obtained by compiling one definitive ENRICHI in advance, while preserving the historical source documents and mappings independently.

**D1-P3300** · My preferred solution is therefore:

**D1-P3301** · One canonical published corpus, one common source for search and reading, and one permanent structured editorial archive.

**D1-P3302** · I would make that the proposed future architecture, subject to a bounded feasibility test.

**D1-P3303** · 2. The fundamental problem with the existing system

**D1-P3304** · Today, we effectively have several representations of the same underlying material.

**D1-P3305** · Current v142.19 architecture — simplified

**D1-P3306** · PRINCIPAL

**D1-P3307** · 74,351 paragraphs

**D1-P3308** · COMPLÉMENTS

**D1-P3316** · There is a separate search-build process, rather than a single demonstrated byte-equivalent text contract shared across all functions.

**D1-P3317** · The current Reader's buildEnrichedReaderUnits() function takes the Principal paragraphs, the supplement placement index and the grouping information, then builds the text to display.

**D1-P3318** · For a supplement inserted within a paragraph, it divides the canonical paragraph at canonical_left_end and canonical_right_start, inserts the supplement fragments, and then resumes displaying the Principal.

**D1-P3319** · That design is flexible. It also has a fundamental weakness:

**D1-P3320** · It depends on insertion coordinates remaining correct whenever the underlying Principal is amended.

**D1-P3321** · That is directly relevant to the three mid-word defects discovered in v142.19, including the transforme, éteint and Mienne boundaries.

**D1-P3322** · A valid historical fragment can acquire an invalid position after the host text is corrected.

**D1-P3323** · There is a second, more subtle problem. Even when the insertion coordinate remains valid, the resulting text may no longer be grammatically correct or editorially necessary. The Tome 7 January 1906 F04 issue illustrates this.

**D1-P3324** · The problem is not that having documentary sources is inherently wrong. It is that documentary relationships are being used as live instructions for constructing the definitive reading.

**D1-P3325** · Those responsibilities should be separated.

**D1-P3349** · The model is multilingual-e5-small, a pretrained multilingual embedding model.

**D1-P3350** · We are not training the model on the Livre du Ciel. We are preparing passages, generating embeddings and constructing an index against which readers' questions are evaluated.

**D1-P3351** · That distinction changes the expected benefit.

**D1-P3352** · There would be no need to retrain a new language model merely because we adopt one ENRICHI. Nor would we automatically eliminate two-thirds of the model files or inference time.

**D1-P3353** · The benefits would arise from making the data pipeline more reliable.

**D1-P3354** · What would genuinely improve

**D1-P3355** · A. One unambiguous input corpus

**D1-P3356** · Today, editorially related Principal and supplementary passages can be represented differently in the Reader and search indexes.

**D1-P3357** · With one ENRICHI, we would know exactly what words every search index should contain.

**D1-P3358** · B. No unintended duplicate translations in normal search

**D1-P3359** · The R91C investigation has identified cases where a supplement repeats material already present in the corrected Principal.

**D1-P3360** · A canonical reading could include the approved wording once, keeping the alternative translation in the historical apparatus.

**D1-P3361** · This might improve ranking by reducing redundant passages. However, the extent of the improvement must be measured; it cannot be assumed.

**D1-P3362** · C. Exact validation of source coverage

**D1-P3363** · Every approved canonical passage should have an explicit mapping into the lexical and semantic source documents.

**D1-P3364** · The compiler could detect omitted characters, incorrectly joined fragments and unsupported source-span boundaries before any application is released.

**D1-P3365** · D. Much simpler future corrections

**D1-P3366** · When a textual correction is approved, it changes the canonical reading.

**D1-P3367** · The build process then identifies its effects on the lexical index, semantic chunks, speaker ranges and navigation mappings.

**D1-P3368** · This replaces a significant portion of the current manual reconciliation.

**D1-P3369** · What would not automatically improve

**D1-P3370** · One ENRICHI would not, by itself, solve:

**D1-P3371** · Weak semantic ranking for certain natural-language queries.

**D1-P3372** · Incorrect confidence calibration or result ordering.

**D1-P3373** · Loading delays associated with the ONNX model.

**D1-P3374** · Network-transfer and memory behaviour on particular devices.

**D1-P3375** · Ambiguous or incomplete Jesus-attribution metadata.

**D1-P3376** · Those remain separate engineering and evaluation questions.

**D1-P3377** · Therefore, I expect a material improvement in search maintainability and source correctness, but I would not predict a major increase in search speed merely from merging the text.

**D1-P3378** · 5. The more significant benefit may actually be outside Par le sens

**D1-P3379** · The current code contains roughly 94 references to supplementMode in index.html. That is a crude indicator of coupling, not 94 independent defects.

**D1-P3380** · The source-mode choice influences:

**D1-P3381** · Library entry selection and counts.

**D1-P3382** · Reader presentation.

**D1-P3383** · Lexical search scope and filters.

**D1-P3384** · Speaker-data composition.

**D1-P3385** · Navigation and return-position restoration.

**D1-P3386** · Reading positions and source-mode preferences.

**D1-P3387** · Documentary information shown alongside notes and selected passages.

**D1-P3388** · The code's setSupplementMode() function must preserve or rebuild substantial application state when switching between Principal, Compléments and ENRICHI.

**D1-P3389** · This is a much broader engineering burden than the source-text assembly alone.

**D1-P3390** · Removing the ability to switch between three full reading views could eventually remove many of these branches and reduce future regression risks.

**D1-P3391** · However, simply hiding the documentary-view selector would not remove that underlying complexity. The internal contracts would have to be simplified carefully.

**D1-P3392** · This is why I recommend treating one canonical text and retirement of the extra reading modes as two separate implementation steps.

**D1-P3393** · We could achieve the main reliability benefits first, then remove unused mode-specific behaviour once its dependencies are fully understood.

**D1-P3394** · 6. The crucial question: what exactly do we mean by “one ENRICHI”?

**D1-P3395** · There are three materially different options.

**D1-T060-R01** · Architecture | Editorial safety | Long-term simplicity | Assessment

**D1-T060-R02** · A. Merge everything into a single plain text, retaining only written documentation | Weak | Appears simple, but creates future tracing problems | Reject

**D1-T060-R03** · B. One definitive ENRICHI for the app, with structured provenance and variants preserved externally | Strong if properly validated | High | Preferred end state

**D1-T060-R04** · C. Keep three internal source layers, but compile one definitive ENRICHI for reading and searching | Strong | High for the core text pipeline; less simplification of documentary modes | Preferred transition

**D1-P3396** · My strongest recommendation is C leading to B, rather than immediately doing B as a full rewrite.

**D1-P3397** · This distinction is important because the historical editorial record contains decisions that cannot safely be reduced to a plain paragraph of French.

**D1-P3398** · Example: Tome 20, 1 January 1927

**D1-P3399** · The historical R6 investigation favoured a reading based on the IT-DV transmission, involving the Divine Will flowing through the cut.

**D1-P3400** · The later R2 correction supports the current Principal wording, which describes the Divine Will beginning its life again in the cut.

**D1-P3401** · We should eventually select one approved French wording for the normal ENRICHI.

**D1-P3402** · But the competing Italian readings and historical decisions should remain available.

**D1-P3403** · The correct structure would be:

**D1-P3404** · Canonical published reading: the selected French text.

**D1-P3405** · Editorial apparatus: the alternative IT-DV reading, original source references, historical R6 approval, subsequent R2 correction, rationale for choosing the current text and preserved fragment ID.

**D1-P3406** · A reader can enjoy a continuous text without seeing two competing translations inserted sequentially.

**D1-P3407** · A researcher can still examine precisely what happened.

**D1-P3408** · Example: Tome 7, January 1906

**D1-P3409** · We already know that the F01/F02 relationship must be adjudicated atomically and that F04 creates a separate grammatical problem.

**D1-P3410** · A single text does not eliminate the need to resolve those editorial questions.

**D1-P3411** · Indeed, the danger would be to flatten the currently defective ENRICHI and accidentally make those defects permanent.

**D1-P3412** · The correct sequence is source reconciliation, approved composite text, and then deterministic publication.

**D1-P3413** · 7. How to preserve all the historical work

**D1-P3414** · I would not rely solely on a comprehensive Word document, however good it might be.

**D1-P3415** · We need two complementary forms of documentation.

**D1-P3416** · Human-readable documentation

**D1-P3417** · A detailed source-critical record explaining why each change was made, what the original text said, which witnesses were considered and which decisions were approved.

**D1-P3418** · This can remain in Word and Markdown, with full cumulative history.

**D1-P3419** · Structured editorial provenance

**D1-P3420** · A machine-readable register with, for each textual operation:

**D1-T061-R01** · Field | Purpose

**D1-T061-R02** · Canonical passage ID | Stable identity in the definitive ENRICHI

**D1-T061-R03** · Original Principal paragraph ID | Link to its historical corpus origin

**D1-T061-R04** · Supplement/fragment ID | Preservation of original supplement identity

**D1-T061-R05** · Exact source span | Identify which words came from which source or operation

**D1-T061-R06** · Historical authorisation | Identify the governing R6/R2 or other approved decision

**D1-T061-R07** · Editorial role | Addition, correction, overlapping translation or documentary variant

**D1-T061-R08** · Effective published text hash | Detect unexpected changes

**D1-T061-R09** · Legacy reference mapping | Preserve bookmarks, highlights, notes and links

**D1-P3421** · For ordinary Principal text, much of this mapping is straightforward.

**D1-P3422** · For within-paragraph supplements, it requires care. A single resulting sentence may contain words derived from more than one source record.

**D1-P3423** · We therefore need provenance at the relevant text-span level, not merely a note saying that the paragraph contains supplementary material.

**D1-P3424** · This is the central technical safeguard that makes the proposed architecture defensible.

**D1-P3425** · 8. The biggest migration risk: user data

**D1-P3426** · This deserves more attention than it received in my earlier analysis.

**D1-P3427** · The existing Reader was deliberately designed to preserve highlights and reading positions against the full, unsplit canonical paragraph text, even where a supplement divides that paragraph visually.

**D1-P3428** · The frozen code explicitly maintains this distinction.

**D1-P3429** · In addition, persisted reading-position records can include the paragraph ID, supplement ID, source mode and position within the paragraph.

**D1-P3430** · If we replace the existing paragraph-and-fragment structure with new flattened paragraph IDs, those relationships may cease to resolve correctly.

**D1-P3431** · Consider a user who has highlighted words belonging to a supplement inserted midway through a Principal paragraph.

**D1-P3432** · Under the proposed ENRICHI, those words might now be part of one continuous paragraph.

**D1-P3433** · We must still be able to establish:

**D1-P3434** · Which historical supplement the highlight originally belonged to.

**D1-P3435** · Which precise words it covers in the new canonical text.

**D1-P3436** · Whether it was part of a variant no longer displayed inline.

**D1-P3437** · Where the Reader should navigate when the user opens it.

**D1-P3438** · A simple character-offset shift is insufficient if earlier words have been replaced or a complete fragment has moved into the documentary apparatus.

**D1-P3439** · The solution is not to preserve three reading modes forever. It is to preserve a versioned, bidirectional identity and text-span mapping.

**D1-P3440** · The migration must be able to translate old locations to the new canonical text and, where necessary, back to the historical source.

**D1-P3441** · For ambiguous mappings, user records must be retained and flagged rather than silently attached to the wrong words.

**D1-P3442** · I would require zero unexplained orphaned records in the controlled migration tests before approving the architecture.

**D1-P3443** · This is probably the most demanding part of the transition, not generating the new semantic embeddings.

**D1-P3444** · 9. Would this reduce application size and improve loading performance?

**D1-P3445** · Probably not substantially.

**D1-P3446** · I calculated the asset distribution directly from the frozen v142.19 application ZIP.

**D1-T062-R01** · Asset group | Uncompressed size | Compressed within ZIP

**D1-T062-R02** · Corpus assets, including textual search data | 114.48 MB | 17.87 MB

**D1-T062-R03** · Semantic model and tokenizer assets | 140.21 MB | 85.72 MB

**D1-T062-R04** · Semantic pack | 50.52 MB | 13.99 MB

**D1-P3447** · These categories describe file contents within the supplied ZIP, not exact device network-transfer amounts.

**D1-P3448** · The model is already shared. Its size does not depend on whether the Reader exposes one or three documentary views.

**D1-P3449** · The supplements themselves are a small proportion of the corpus—177 paragraphs relative to 74,351 Principal paragraphs. Their complexity is disproportionate to their size because of the placement, provenance and state dependencies.

**D1-P3450** · The realistic benefits are therefore:

**D1-P3451** · Fewer runtime composition paths.

**D1-P3452** · Fewer opportunities for text/index divergence.

**D1-P3453** · Simpler release verification.

**D1-P3454** · Less maintenance when correcting the corpus.

**D1-P3455** · Potentially fewer duplicated search passages.

**D1-P3456** · There may be secondary performance improvements, but they should be established through benchmarks rather than promised in advance.

**D1-P3457** · 10. Could we avoid a risky rewrite?

**D1-P3458** · Yes. This is the most important improvement to my recommendation.

**D1-P3459** · We should not start by deleting the Principal and Compléments structures or replacing all the existing paragraph IDs.

**D1-P3460** · Instead, build a read-only canonical compiler using the frozen source material.

**D1-P3461** · This compiler would generate a static ENRICHI containing the complete approved text of all 36 tomes, preserving dates, entry IDs and existing paragraph identities wherever possible.

**D1-P3462** · It would additionally produce a provenance map and explicit legacy-reference map.

**D1-P3463** · At first, this would be an independent research artifact. The deployed application would not change.

**D1-P3464** · We could then compare that static output with the Reader's present ENRICHI.

**D1-P3465** · The decisive feasibility test

**D1-P3466** · The following questions should be answered empirically:

**D1-T063-R01** · Test | Required outcome

**D1-T063-R02** · Complete coverage | All approved entries and paragraphs represented

**D1-T063-R03** · Existing-text equivalence | No unexplained differences outside documented corrections

**D1-T063-R04** · Documentary completeness | Every approved supplement and variant accounted for

**D1-T063-R05** · Stable references | Every valid existing reference resolves or has an explicit migration mapping

**D1-T063-R06** · Source provenance | Every editorial addition and correction remains traceable

**D1-T063-R07** · Speaker attribution | Ranges correctly mapped to the effective text

**D1-T063-R08** · Lexical and semantic inputs | Both reproducibly generated from the same canonical version

**D1-T063-R09** · Annotation migration | No silent data loss, misattachment or unintended modification

**D1-P3467** · An especially valuable test would be a mutation test: deliberately alter a copied source paragraph after compiling the ENRICHI, then verify that the build-integrity controls detect the mismatch and refuse to publish dependent search assets.

**D1-P3468** · That would demonstrate that we have addressed the actual class of problem, rather than simply moved it somewhere else.

**D1-P3469** · The important architectural distinction

**D1-P3470** · One canonical corpus does not have to mean one enormous undifferentiated string.

**D1-P3471** · I would keep 36 tomes, dated entries, stable paragraphs and span-level references.

**D1-P3472** · What becomes singular is the authority of the published wording, not its physical storage structure.

**D1-P3473** · That gives us the benefits of simplification without sacrificing normal navigation, performance or provenance.

**D1-P3474** · 11. The proposed execution plan

**D1-P3475** · I would make the decision through four controlled stages.

**D1-P3476** · 1

**D1-P3477** · Complete the editorial source review

**D1-P3478** · Review the 75 supplements against the corrected Principal, finish the seven disputed cases, and resolve any additional justified defects. Classify each fragment as integrated text, superseded duplication or documentary variant.

**D1-P3479** · Output: One proposed authoritative text contract, with unresolved decisions explicitly identified.

**D1-P3480** · 2

**D1-P3481** · Prove the single-ENRICHI architecture read-only

**D1-P3482** · Develop an independent compiler and source map without touching production. Measure exact textual equivalence, preservation of stable IDs, legacy-mapping coverage and the amount of application complexity it would actually remove.

**D1-P3483** · This stage can be undertaken in parallel with editorial adjudication using the frozen current corpus, then repeated with the approved corrected text.

**D1-P3484** · Output: A factual feasibility assessment and quantified migration-risk inventory.

**D1-P3485** · 3

**D1-P3486** · Owner architecture and implementation decision

**D1-P3487** · Compare the verified result with the simpler alternative of retaining the existing architecture and repairing the known discrepancies.

**D1-P3488** · Authorise a single-ENRICHI successor only if the prototype demonstrates meaningful reliability and maintenance benefits without unacceptable data-migration risks.

**D1-P3489** · Output: A bounded, approved implementation specification.

**D1-P3490** · 4

**D1-P3491** · Implement and qualify separately

**D1-P3492** · Generate the canonical text and search assets in an isolated successor. Preserve the model unless independent retrieval evidence supports changing it. Test navigation, notes, highlights, variants, search ranking, service worker behaviour and physical iPhone/iPad performance.

**D1-P3493** · Output: A release candidate, with deployment subject to separate approval.

**D1-P3494** · The principal remaining uncertainty is not whether a static canonical text is technically possible. It is whether the full migration can be achieved without damaging established reader-state behaviour, while delivering enough simplification to justify the architectural change.

**D1-P3495** · That uncertainty can be substantially reduced through the read-only feasibility test, without rebuilding or deploying the application.

**D1-P3496** · 12. Decision comparison

**D1-T064-R01** · Criterion | Repair existing architecture | Single compiled ENRICHI with retained provenance

**D1-T064-R02** · Resolve the seven known editorial cases | Yes | Yes

**D1-T064-R03** · Address future stale runtime insertion offsets | Requires continuing controls | Eliminates runtime dependency on them

**D1-T064-R04** · Ensure Reader/search text equivalence | Requires cross-pipeline checks | One source makes this easier to enforce

**D1-T064-R05** · Reduce source-mode complexity | Limited | Potentially substantial

**D1-T064-R06** · Preserve scholarly provenance | Already supported | Requires robust source-map design

**D1-T064-R07** · Preserve existing annotations | Lower immediate risk | Significant migration requirements

**D1-T064-R08** · Short-term development effort | Lower | Higher

**D1-T064-R09** · Long-term maintenance | More complex | Likely simpler

**D1-T064-R10** · Improve semantic model performance automatically | No | No

**D1-T064-R11** · Overall assessment | Safe short-term fallback | Preferred strategic direction if feasibility gates pass

**D1-P3497** · 13. Final recommendation

**D1-P3498** · I am more confident about the architectural direction after inspecting the frozen implementation. I am also more cautious about the order in which it should be executed.

**D1-P3499** · I recommend adopting one canonical ENRICHI as the intended long-term architecture, but not yet authorising a wholesale replacement of the existing application.

**D1-P3500** · The key strategic choices are:

**D1-P3501** · One published text: yes.

**D1-P3502** · One shared Reader and search source: yes.

**D1-P3503** · No live construction of the definitive reading from stale supplement offsets: yes.

**D1-P3504** · Retain all historical source evidence and editorial variants: essential.

**D1-P3505** · Retain three permanent user-facing reading modes: probably unnecessary.

**D1-P3506** · Flatten away historical IDs, text-span mappings or provenance: no.

**D1-P3507** · Retrain the semantic model: unnecessary unless separate evidence justifies it.

**D1-P3508** · Rewrite v142.19 immediately: no.

**D1-P3509** · What I would authorise now

**D1-P3510** · Two parallel read-only workstreams:

**D1-P3511** · Editorial: finish the full supplement reconciliation and establish the approved definitive ENRICHI.

**D1-P3512** · Technical: independently compile the existing ENRICHI into a single static, source-mapped corpus and determine precisely what it would take to preserve existing functionality and user data.

**D1-P3513** · This should give us a decision grounded in actual migration evidence, rather than an assumption that fewer textual views necessarily means a simpler application.

**D1-P3514** · The key insight: The long-term goal should not be to maintain three texts correctly forever. It should be to maintain one authoritative published text correctly, with every editorial decision traceable to its historical sources.

**D1-P3515** · analyse further. dig much deeper

**D1-P3516** · Worked for 5m 13s

**D1-P3517** · Livre du Ciel — Deeper architectural assessment

**D1-P3518** · 1. My revised conclusion

**D1-P3519** · I increasingly favour one definitive ENRICHI, but the best solution is not simply to merge three bodies of text. It is to change how the authoritative text is established, versioned, verified and delivered to the Reader and search engines.

**D1-P3520** · Having examined the frozen v142.19 application, its supplement registry, lexical search topology, semantic model configuration and existing user-data mechanisms, I would distinguish three separate decisions:

**D1-P3521** · Editorial: What is the definitive French text that users should read?

**D1-P3522** · Architectural: How do we ensure that reading, lexical search and semantic search all use that same approved text?

**D1-P3523** · Product: Should users retain the ability to switch between Principal, Compléments and ENRICHI?

**D1-P3524** · These questions have been intertwined in the existing application. Separating them reveals an important opportunity.

**D1-P3525** · We can obtain most of the technical reliability benefits of one ENRICHI before deciding whether to remove the other two documentary views.

**D1-P3526** · I would now recommend a staged transition to a single canonical publication system, retaining source distinctions as structured evidence rather than as competing authorities for normal reading.

**D1-P3527** · This is a stronger and safer proposal than immediately flattening the corpus and rewriting the application.

**D1-P3528** · 2. Important new findings from the actual v142.19 files

**D1-P3529** · I independently rechecked the frozen application archive.

**D1-P3530** · Principal paragraphs

**D1-P3531** · 74,351

**D1-P3532** · Supplement items

**D1-P3533** · 75

**D1-P3534** · Placement contracts

**D1-P3535** · 76

**D1-P3536** · Semantic passages

**D1-P3537** · 22,873

**D1-P3538** · Verified against the frozen v142.19 archive, SHA-256 beginning 3826f8ab, ZIP CRC PASS.

**D1-P3539** · The actual lexical topology also contains:

**D1-P3540** · 62 enriched-entry overrides;

**D1-P3541** · 13 complete supplementary entries;

**D1-P3544** · 1,052 lexical-display operations.

**D1-P3545** · This is significant. The complexity is not simply the presence of three French texts. It is the number of transformations and mappings through which the final text passes.

**D1-P3546** · The Reader dynamically assembles the ENRICHI. The lexical search engine has its own topology, while the semantic engine uses 96-word windows with a 72-word stride.

**D1-P3547** · They can legitimately represent text at different granularities. What should not differ is the underlying approved wording and provenance.

**D1-P3548** · An instructive technical detail

**D1-P3549** · I found four placement contracts where the right-hand canonical offset exceeds the left-hand offset by one character. Three are ordinary within-paragraph placements; the fourth is a special placement following a Principal correction.

**D1-P3550** · I checked the actual host paragraphs. All four skipped characters are spaces, not words or theological statements.

**D1-P3551** · That does not establish that the joins are correctly spaced after composition, but it substantially reduces the concern that this mechanism is silently deleting substantive text in those four cases.

**D1-P3552** · It also illustrates the value of replacing runtime fragment manipulation with a prevalidated published text: an editorial compiler could check such joins once, rather than relying on every Reader composition to reproduce them correctly.

**D1-P3553** · 3. A critical correction to the expected benefits for search

**D1-P3554** · The deeper code inspection changes my assessment of how much complexity would disappear from the two search engines.

**D1-P3555** · Par les mots already uses one underlying document population

**D1-P3556** · In search_engine_v2.js, the lexical engine loads one set of documents and applies source-mode filters.

**D1-P3557** · The relevant logic is effectively:

**D1-P3558** · Principal: accept Principal records.

**D1-P3559** · Compléments: accept supplementary records.

**D1-P3560** · ENRICHI: accept both.

**D1-P3561** · It does not maintain three entirely separate lexical indexes.

**D1-P3562** · Similarly, Par le sens already operates on an ENRICHI semantic pack.

**D1-P3563** · Therefore:

**D1-P3564** · Removing the three reading modes does not eliminate two redundant search engines or two redundant sets of embeddings.

**D1-P3565** · The benefits would be concentrated elsewhere:

**D1-P3566** · Eliminating the need to reconcile several interpretations of the final text.

**D1-P3567** · Preventing stale supplementary positions from affecting reading.

**D1-P3568** · Making source coverage and speaker attribution easier to validate.

**D1-P3569** · Simplifying navigation, search-result destinations and source-mode changes.

**D1-P3570** · Establishing one reliable process for future editorial corrections.

**D1-P3571** · This is still valuable. But I would no longer describe it as a major simplification of the underlying semantic-search algorithm.

**D1-P3572** · It is primarily a data-integrity and application-architecture improvement.

**D1-P3573** · 4. Which problems would disappear, and which would remain?

**D1-P3574** · This is the most important causal test of the proposal.

**D1-T065-R01** · Current problem | Effect of one compiled ENRICHI

**D1-T065-R02** · Stale runtime supplement insertion positions | Largely eliminated once compilation and approval are complete

**D1-T065-R03** · Reader/search disagreements about text | Much easier to prevent, provided all assets are generated and verified together

**D1-T065-R04** · Supplement duplicates already corrected Principal | Still requires editorial adjudication first

**D1-T065-R05** · Inaccurate French translations | Not solved

**D1-T065-R06** · Incorrect Jesus-attribution ranges | Not solved, but one common coordinate system simplifies repair

**D1-T065-R07** · Semantic-index coverage omissions | Not automatically solved; requires explicit coverage checks

**D1-T065-R08** · Poor semantic ranking | Not solved

**D1-T065-R09** · ONNX loading and memory problems | Essentially unaffected

**D1-T065-R10** · Source genealogy and competing translations | Still requires permanent documentary records

**D1-T065-R11** · Highlights, annotations and old links | New migration risk during conversion

**D1-T065-R12** · Future release inconsistencies | Reduced if build manifests and cache versions are verified atomically

**D1-P3575** · This reveals a possible mistake in the broader simplification proposal.

**D1-P3576** · The seven cases were not principally caused by the existence of three reading modes.

**D1-P3577** · They arose from interactions between changing Principal text, historical supplementary material, placement coordinates and independently generated search representations.

**D1-P3578** · We could retain three views and still correct those mechanisms.

**D1-P3579** · Conversely, we could remove two views but continue generating Reader and search assets independently—and reproduce essentially the same inconsistencies.

**D1-P3580** · Therefore, the highest-value reform is one authoritative build and publication contract, not merely one visible text.

**D1-P3581** · 5. The architectural choice is actually between three viable approaches

**D1-P3582** · Option A — Repair the existing system

**D1-P3583** · Lowest migration risk

**D1-P3584** · Keep all three modes. Correct the seven cases, review remaining supplements, and strengthen source-offset and index-integrity checks.

**D1-P3585** · Strength: Preserves all current functionality and user-data assumptions.

**D1-P3586** · Weakness: Retains much of the complex source-mode and runtime-composition architecture.

**D1-P3587** · Option B — Compile one canonical ENRICHI

**D1-P3588** · Preferred first step

**D1-P3589** · Preserve the historical source records, but compile a definitive ENRICHI at build time. Reader and both search engines derive their content from this common publication version. Keep existing documentary views temporarily for migration compatibility.

**D1-P3590** · Strength: Addresses the central source-integrity risks while controlling the migration.

**D1-P3591** · Weakness: Some legacy source-mode code remains until it can be safely retired.

**D1-P3592** · Option C — One published ENRICHI only

**D1-P3593** · Preferred long-term goal

**D1-P3594** · Build on Option B. Remove the two documentary reading modes from normal application workflows. Retain historical sources, variants and reference mappings as an independent editorial apparatus.

**D1-P3595** · Strength: Cleaner product, simpler navigation and fewer permanent dependencies.

**D1-P3596** · Weakness: Requires a proven legacy-data migration and careful handling of old documentary links.

**D1-P3597** · I would not jump directly from A to C.

**D1-P3598** · Option B is the decisive step. It gives us an opportunity to measure whether C would provide enough additional benefit to justify removing the remaining mode-specific functionality.

**D1-P3599** · 6. A better definition of the future ENRICHI

**D1-P3600** · The future text should not simply be the concatenation of all 74,351 Principal and 177 supplementary paragraphs.

**D1-P3601** · It should be an editorially established reading.

**D1-P3602** · Each dated entry would have one approved continuous French text. Genuine additions would be integrated at their correct positions. Alternative translations would be available in the documentary apparatus rather than repeated inside the continuous reading.

**D1-P3603** · Four particularly important design requirements follow.

**D1-P3604** · A. Preserve complete supplementary entries as genuine entries

**D1-P3605** · There are 13 complete supplementary entries in the current registry.

**D1-P3606** · These are different from a supplementary phrase inserted into an existing paragraph.

**D1-P3607** · If an entire dated entry is genuinely absent from the Principal, it should remain a distinct dated entry in the canonical ENRICHI.

**D1-P3608** · It must not be swallowed by the preceding or following entry merely to eliminate the supplement classification.

**D1-P3609** · Its historical source identity should remain accessible.

**D1-P3610** · B. Distinguish source identity from published identity

**D1-P3611** · A passage may have two distinct identities:

**D1-P3612** · Its historical source identity: for example, the original SUP-T2 fragment.

**D1-P3613** · Its published reading identity: the location where the approved text now appears in the definitive ENRICHI.

**D1-P3614** · Both should be stable.

**D1-P3615** · The source identifier records provenance. The published identifier controls reading, searching, bookmarking and navigation.

**D1-P3616** · A permanent cross-reference must link them.

**D1-P3617** · C. Preserve variants without repeating them in ordinary reading

**D1-P3618** · For Tome 20, the current Principal and the historical R6-derived fragment should not automatically both appear in the main continuous text.

**D1-P3619** · The eventual editorial decision should select the published reading while preserving the alternative in a source note.

**D1-P3620** · This is an important distinction: preserving a text does not require displaying it inline as a second continuation of the passage.

**D1-P3621** · The app could retain a simple Sources et variantes control for interested readers without retaining two separate complete documentary reading modes.

**D1-P3622** · D. Never describe the composite as an unmodified original

**D1-P3623** · A source-critically established ENRICHI combines a historical French corpus, verified corrections and additions drawn from identified sources.

**D1-P3624** · It should be described accurately as an editorially established reading of the Livre du Ciel, with documented source provenance.

**D1-P3625** · That preserves scholarly honesty and avoids implying that the resulting French text is an unmodified transcription of a single source edition.

**D1-P3626** · 7. The biggest hidden technical requirement: text-span provenance

**D1-P3627** · My earlier analysis emphasised historical documentation. I would now make the requirement more precise.

**D1-P3628** · We need to preserve provenance at the level of the actual words and text spans that make up the definitive ENRICHI.

**D1-P3629** · A paragraph-level note alone is insufficient where a supplement contributes only part of a sentence.

**D1-P3630** · For example, a single published paragraph might consist of:

**D1-P3631** · Illustrative published passage structure

**D1-P3632** · Principal text A

**D1-P3633** · Approved supplementary material

**D1-P3634** · Principal text B

**D1-P3635** · Provenance sidecar, not separate reading modes

**D1-P3636** · Each span retains its source ID, historical decision, original text hash, published coordinates and alternative-witness references.

**D1-P3637** · This gives us a coherent single text without losing its genealogy.

**D1-P3638** · The trade-off is that the source register becomes more sophisticated. But that complexity would live largely in the editorial preparation and build process, not in the everyday Reader or search interface.

**D1-P3639** · That is where it belongs.

**D1-P3640** · 8. The user-data problem is more extensive than highlights

**D1-P3641** · The frozen application maintains eight persistent user-data stores:

**D1-P3642** · reading_pos, highlights, notes, favorites, collections, col_items, settings and read_entries.

**D1-P3643** · The documentary mode also appears in navigation transactions and reading-session state.

**D1-P3644** · In addition, public search links can explicitly encode src=principal, src=complement or src=enrichi.

**D1-P3645** · This creates several migration obligations.

**D1-T066-R01** · Existing object | Required treatment in single-ENRICHI

**D1-T066-R02** · Principal paragraph reference | Normally retain the same stable identity

**D1-T066-R03** · Integrated supplement reference | Redirect to its precise canonical location

**D1-T066-R04** · Documentary variant reference | Open the preserved variant, not an unrelated canonical passage

**D1-T066-R05** · Highlight over a moved fragment | Re-anchor to the same words, or retain as unresolved

**D1-T066-R06** · Saved note attached to a variant | Preserve original source and association

**D1-T066-R07** · Reading position in a supplementary entry | Restore the corresponding canonical dated entry

**D1-T066-R08** · Favourite or read status | Preserve its meaning without double counting

**D1-T066-R09** · Old source-specific search link | Translate source intent or open a documented legacy-source view

**D1-T066-R10** · Exported backup | Remain recoverable under the new schema

**D1-P3646** · A subtle complication is that an old highlight can refer to text which is no longer present inline after editorial de-duplication.

**D1-P3647** · We must not silently attach such a highlight to merely similar words in the new text.

**D1-P3648** · In that situation, the highlight should remain linked to the historical variant, or be explicitly marked for re-anchoring.

**D1-P3649** · Preservation means retaining meaning and ownership of user data, not merely retaining the same number of database records.

**D1-P3650** · This is the strongest argument against a big-bang migration.

**D1-P3651** · 9. One canonical source still requires several derived representations

**D1-P3652** · This is another area where I would refine the proposed architecture.

**D1-P3653** · Having one authoritative text does not mean the Reader, lexical search and semantic search should all consume the identical physical file in the identical format.

**D1-P3654** · Their functions differ.

**D1-P3655** · The Reader needs passage boundaries, typography, speaker presentation and annotation anchors.

**D1-P3656** · Par les mots needs tokenised documents and exact-phrase matching.

**D1-P3657** · Par le sens needs passage windows, embeddings, semantic metadata, filters and a mapping back to the Reader.

**D1-P3658** · The correct relationship is:

**D1-P3659** · Immutable editorial sources

**D1-P3660** · Principal history, supplementary witnesses, variants, approval ledger

**D1-P3661** · Editorial compiler with validation

**D1-P3662** · Transforms only signed, source-supported decisions

**D1-P3663** · Canonical ENRICHI + provenance map

**D1-P3664** · One authoritative text and version identifier

**D1-P3665** · Reader assets

**D1-P3666** · Formatting and stable anchors

**D1-P3667** · Lexical index

**D1-P3668** · Words and exact phrases

**D1-P3669** · Semantic index

**D1-P3670** · Windows and embeddings

**D1-P3671** · One release manifest binds every derived asset to the same approved corpus version.

**D1-P3672** · The compiler should record exact input and output hashes, including the source corpus, editorial decisions, semantic model and relevant tokenisation configuration.

**D1-P3673** · It should not rely on the fact that the semantic metadata happens to contain some text matching the Reader.

**D1-P3674** · The prior R86C investigation already established why this distinction matters: the 41 recorded semantic fingerprints are hashes of metadata text, not proof of the complete model input actually embedded.

**D1-P3675** · An improved architecture needs to validate the real dependency chain, not introduce another set of reassuring but incomplete hashes.

**D1-P3676** · What this means for model rebuilding

**D1-P3677** · Changing the canonical text may shift semantic passage windows.

**D1-P3678** · A small editorial correction can therefore alter embeddings beyond the exact words edited.

**D1-P3679** · It can also change lexical-index statistics and retrieval rankings elsewhere.

**D1-P3680** · The compiler must identify actual dependent changes and rebuild what is necessary. Reusing unrelated, unchanged vectors is desirable, but only where input identity is proved.

**D1-P3681** · No general retraining of multilingual-e5-small is needed.

**D1-P3682** · 10. Would a single ENRICHI solve the seven known cases?

**D1-P3683** · Not by itself.

**D1-P3684** · Consider the two most difficult cases.

**D1-P3685** · Tome 7, January 1906: We still must decide how F01–F04 relate to the corrected Principal and repair any invalid composition. The compiler cannot responsibly invent those editorial choices.

**D1-P3686** · Tome 20, January 1927: We still need to decide which source reading governs the normal text and how the alternative IT-DV transmission will be documented.

**D1-P3687** · The proposed architecture would make those decisions easier to implement correctly and consistently after approval.

**D1-P3688** · It would not determine the decisions.

**D1-P3689** · This leads to an important recommendation: the source-critical review of the 75 supplements should proceed regardless of the architectural outcome.

**D1-P3690** · That work is necessary whether we retain three modes or adopt one ENRICHI.

**D1-P3691** · We should not postpone it while debating the architecture, and we should not use architecture simplification as a reason to reopen the entire 36-tome linguistic audit.

**D1-P3692** · 11. A stronger way to determine whether the change is worthwhile

**D1-P3693** · Rather than estimate the development benefit subjectively, I would conduct a tightly defined, read-only comparison.

**D1-P3694** · Experiment A — Prove text equivalence

**D1-P3695** · Compile a static ENRICHI from the frozen v142.19 sources without making editorial changes.

**D1-P3696** · Compare it against the actual existing Reader-composition contract.

**D1-P3697** · Require exact or structurally explained agreement for all unaffected passages. Maintain a separate list of the already identified defective joins and source conflicts.

**D1-P3698** · This establishes whether the new compiler faithfully reproduces current functionality.

**D1-P3699** · It is not editorial approval of the current defects.

**D1-P3700** · Experiment B — Prove provenance and identity preservation

**D1-P3701** · Account for all:

**D1-P3702** · 74,351 Principal paragraphs.

**D1-P3703** · 177 supplementary paragraphs and their 75 parent items.

**D1-P3704** · 76 placement contracts.

**D1-P3705** · 13 distinct complete supplementary entries.

**D1-P3706** · Current valid stable references and legacy aliases.

**D1-P3707** · Every historical identifier must resolve to its approved published location or to an explicitly preserved documentary variant.

**D1-P3708** · No unaccounted source material should disappear.

**D1-P3709** · Experiment C — Test future correction resilience

**D1-P3710** · Using disposable copies only, deliberately:

**D1-P3711** · Change a Principal paragraph on which a supplement depends.

**D1-P3712** · Move a fragment to an invalid position.

**D1-P3713** · Duplicate a supplementary passage.

**D1-P3714** · Remove part of a canonical entry from the proposed semantic-source representation.

**D1-P3715** · Mismatch the canonical corpus version and semantic index version.

**D1-P3716** · A robust compiler should detect and reject invalid structures and incompatible asset versions.

**D1-P3717** · Duplication requires particular care: a repeated proposition can be editorially legitimate, so the system should flag suspicious duplication for review rather than automatically delete it.

**D1-P3718** · Experiment D — Evaluate user-data migration

**D1-P3719** · Use representative synthetic records covering each user-data store and difficult source-to-canonical mappings.

**D1-P3720** · Test old and new locations, including records attached to variants that no longer appear inline.

**D1-P3721** · No real user data should be rewritten during this experiment.

**D1-P3722** · Require preservation, explicit unresolved status or safe rollback—not silent loss.

**D1-P3723** · Experiment E — Measure actual technical simplification

**D1-P3724** · Finally, quantify:

**D1-P3725** · Source-mode-dependent code that could genuinely be retired.

**D1-P3726** · The number of runtime composition branches removed.

**D1-P3727** · Changes to package size and startup time.

**D1-P3728** · Changes to search-index generation and validation effort.

**D1-P3729** · Remaining provenance and legacy-compatibility requirements.

**D1-P3730** · Search-result relevance and navigation regressions.

**D1-P3731** · This is how we establish whether a single-ENRICHI successor delivers real benefits rather than simply shifting complexity from one part of the application to another.

**D1-P3732** · 12. My decision criteria

**D1-P3733** · I would authorise the architectural transition only if the feasibility work establishes the following.

**D1-T067-R01** · Gate | Required evidence

**D1-T067-R02** · Editorial completeness | Every supplement has a justified disposition; unresolved variants are explicitly identified

**D1-T067-R03** · Text integrity | No unexplained differences between approved canonical text and published Reader content

**D1-T067-R04** · Source provenance | Every integrated correction, addition and variant remains traceable

**D1-T067-R05** · Stable identity | Every valid legacy paragraph and supplement reference remains resolvable

**D1-T067-R06** · User data | No silent data loss or incorrect re-anchoring in the migration tests

**D1-T067-R07** · Search consistency | Reader, lexical documents and semantic passages derive from the same approved corpus

**D1-T067-R08** · Search quality | Independent evaluation detects no unacceptable retrieval or navigation regression

**D1-T067-R09** · Release integrity | Version, cache, service worker and search assets remain mutually compatible

**D1-T067-R10** · Net benefit | Measurably reduced runtime complexity and maintenance burden without disproportionate migration risk

**D1-P3734** · The net-benefit gate is important.

**D1-P3735** · There are only 75 supplement items. Even though their handling is complex, it does not follow that removing the entire documentary-mode architecture is necessarily worth a high-risk rewrite.

**D1-P3736** · If the feasibility experiment shows that the main problems can be solved through build-time compilation while keeping legacy documentary access, that may be the most economical end state.

**D1-P3737** · We should remain willing to adopt that result.

**D1-P3738** · 13. Recommended order of work

**D1-P3739** · I would now restructure the project into three workstreams, with a clear dependency between them.

**D1-P3740** · Workstream 1 — Editorial closure

**D1-P3741** · Complete the 75-supplement review using the recovered sources. Resolve E01–E07, especially Tome 7 January and Tome 20. Define the exact authoritative continuous French reading and treatment of documentary variants.

**D1-P3742** · This is necessary work, independent of the architecture decision.

**D1-P3743** · Workstream 2 — Read-only canonical-compiler feasibility

**D1-P3744** · Prototype one static ENRICHI and its provenance/legacy mapping from the frozen source. Demonstrate source completeness, equivalence, negative-test behaviour and migration feasibility without touching the deployed application.

**D1-P3745** · This can proceed in parallel with editorial closure.

**D1-P3746** · Workstream 3 — Implementation and release

**D1-P3747** · Only after both earlier workstreams have produced evidence, decide between retaining the existing architecture with stronger guards and implementing a canonical-ENRICHI successor. Require separate authorisation for application mutation, independent testing and deployment.

**D1-P3748** · No change to v142.19 or ongoing independent search prototypes is implied.

**D1-P3749** · I would not combine wholesale architecture migration, editorial corrections and unrelated Par le sens ranking improvements in an unqualified release.

**D1-P3750** · Their effects need to be separately attributable, even if the final approved successor ultimately includes more than one category of change.

**D1-P3751** · 14. Final recommendation

**D1-P3752** · My position is now:

**D1-P3753** · One authoritative ENRICHI is the preferred architectural objective, but the immediately justified action is to prove a single canonical publication pipeline—not to delete the three-view system yet.

**D1-P3754** · The reason is important.

**D1-P3755** · We have accumulated extensive source-critical evidence across 36 tomes. The historical record is valuable and should be protected. But the everyday application should not have to reconstruct the editorial history every time it displays or searches a passage.

**D1-P3756** · That work should be done once, in a controlled editorial build, with a precise source map and immutable approval records.

**D1-P3757** · The Reader and both search systems should then depend on that approved publication.

**D1-P3758** · Once that is working, the Principal-only and Compléments-only modes can be assessed for retirement. Their removal becomes a relatively bounded product simplification rather than a prerequisite for correcting the corpus.

**D1-P3759** · What matters most: exact editorial authority, one common publication text, traceable provenance, stable user references and reproducible dependent search assets.

**D1-P3760** · What matters less: whether historical source records are stored as three files, 36 files or a structured archive. That is not the underlying reliability problem.

**D1-P3761** · The main uncertainty: the cost and safety of preserving all existing user-data and navigation semantics through the transition.

**D1-P3762** · The next decisive action: complete the remaining supplement adjudication and, in parallel, run a read-only single-ENRICHI compiler feasibility study with strict equivalence and migration gates.

**D1-P3763** · If both succeed, I would recommend proceeding towards the new architecture. If migration risks remain material, I would retain documentary compatibility while still adopting the common canonical text pipeline.

**D1-P3764** · Top of Form

**D1-P3766** · Bottom of Form

**D2-P0277** · Worked for 46s

**D2-P0278** · R99 — Réintégration des sources espagnoles et révision de la méthode

**D2-P0279** · Vous avez raison sur un point essentiel : le texte français ne doit pas être présumé correct simplement parce qu'il constitue actuellement le PRINCIPAL de l'application. Ce serait confondre une décision historique de publication avec une preuve de fidélité au texte de Luisa.

**D2-P0280** · J'ai retrouvé dans nos archives l'édition espagnole complète de Thomassiny, Libro de Cielo, 36 volumes, ainsi que les deux familles de textes italiens IT-PM et IT-DV.

**D2-P0281** · Un élément particulièrement intéressant figure dans l'introduction espagnole : l'éditeur affirme avoir traduit directement à partir des manuscrits originaux, tout en reconnaissant que sa traduction est préliminaire et contient des imperfections et probablement des erreurs de transcription. Cette revendication constitue une information de provenance importante, mais pas encore une preuve vérifiée d'accès direct aux manuscrits.

**D2-P0282** · Premiers résultats avec l'espagnol

**D2-T008-R01** · Cas | Constat après confrontation

**D2-T008-R02** · E10 — Tome 7, 11 août 1906 | L'espagnol utilise llaves (« clés »), comme l'italien chiavi. Cela renforce le dossier contre le français verrous.

**D2-T008-R03** · E13 — Tome 3, 25 avril 1900 | L'espagnol confirme que c'est Luisa qui pleure et que Jésus a ensuite compassion d'elle. L'erreur française devient particulièrement convaincante.

**D2-T008-R04** · E14 — Tome 17, 29 juillet 1924 | L'espagnol place su morada, su posesión dans l'énumération initiale, comme les deux éditions italiennes, et non dans sa répétition ultérieure.

**D2-T008-R05** · Tome 15, 2 décembre 1922 | La date n'apparaît pas dans l'édition espagnole sous cette attribution. Le volume 15 espagnol débute le 8 décembre 1922 ; une attribution parallèle au 17 juillet 1923 dans le volume 16 mérite donc une vérification spécifique.

**D2-P0283** · Ces résultats renforcent plusieurs observations antérieures, mais il faut encore vérifier la dépendance éventuelle de l'espagnol à l'égard des éditions italiennes : trois traductions concordantes ne constituent pas forcément trois témoins indépendants.

**D2-P0284** · Une découverte importante : une erreur de datation espagnole

**D2-P0285** · Le complément du 10 mars 1922, Tome 14, semblait absent de l'édition espagnole. Une recherche par le contenu l'a finalement retrouvé, mais avec la date imprimée « Marzo 10, 1923 ».

**D2-P0286** · Le passage parle des Heures de la Passion offertes pour toutes les âmes, exactement comme le complément français. Dans l'édition espagnole, il est situé entre les entrées des 7 et 13 mars 1922.

**D2-P0287** · Cela constitue une forte indication d'une erreur de millésime dans cette édition espagnole. Il serait incorrect de déplacer automatiquement le passage en 1923.

**D2-P0288** · C'est précisément pourquoi la nouvelle méthode doit évaluer les preuves passage par passage, et non choisir une langue ou une édition comme référence infaillible.

**D2-P0289** · Autres conclusions importantes

**D2-P0748** · 2. Principaux résultats éditoriaux

**D2-P0749** · Tome 34 — 18 juin 1937

**D2-P0750** · P004 — Renouvellement de la vie. La traduction française semble effectivement inverser la relation exprimée par les deux versions italiennes. Une correction est proposée, mais l'antécédent grammatical exact reste à arbitrer.

**D2-P0751** · P009 — Omission confirmée. Le français ne reproduit pas l'explication du désir divin de recevoir en retour les baisers et les caresses. Les cinq familles étrangères attestent cette idée, avec des différences de construction.

**D2-P0752** · P010 — Variante italienne réelle. Le fac-similé PM confirme « In tutte », tandis que DV porte « di tutte ». J'ai également identifié une deuxième perte du « I » initial dans l'extraction du texte PM. Les deux lectures éditoriales restent ouvertes.

**D2-P0753** · P008 — Nouvelle divergence découverte. L'italien et l'espagnol expriment l'idée de se brûler soi-même, tandis qu'Owen traduit par « burn Us ». Cette différence mérite une vérification supplémentaire de la traduction française.

**D2-P0754** · Autres dossiers. Les investigations T02, E07 et E09 renforcent la nécessité de distinguer réparation contextuelle, remplacement de texte et ajout de complément, afin d'éviter les duplications.

**D2-P0965** · Circuit B — Assainissement progressif des 75 dossiers

**D2-P0966** · Ce circuit sera organisé par risque et complexité.

**D2-P0970** · Nous ne demanderons une collation philologique exhaustive que lorsque les sources se contredisent, que le sens est réellement incertain ou que le risque éditorial est important.

**D2-P0972** · 5. Ce que nous devons absolument préserver

**D2-P0973** · La rapidité ne doit pas nous conduire à introduire de nouveaux problèmes.

**D2-P0974** · Trois précautions sont essentielles.

**D2-P0975** · La première concerne les sources. Les deux sources italiennes doivent être confrontées dans leur contexte. Ni PM ni DV ne doit être considéré automatiquement comme supérieur. Les traductions espagnoles et anglaises constituent des contrôles supplémentaires, pas un vote permettant de déterminer la bonne lecture.

**D2-P0976** · La deuxième concerne les compléments. Nous ne devons jamais ajouter mécaniquement un passage au texte existant. Lorsqu'une phrase doit être réparée, il faut généralement effectuer une substitution contextualisée plutôt qu'insérer un deuxième texte créant une répétition.

**D2-P0977** · La troisième concerne le fonctionnement de l'application. Toute correction du corpus doit rester cohérente avec la recherche exacte, Par le sens, les identifiants de paragraphes, les annotations des utilisateurs et les données disponibles hors ligne.

**D2-P0978** · Une correction textuelle ne nécessite pas automatiquement de réentraîner le modèle ONNX. En revanche, elle peut nécessiter une mise à jour des index, des représentations sémantiques ou des fichiers dérivés.

**D2-P0979** · Ce point est particulièrement important pour éviter qu'un passage corrigé dans le Reader continue d'apparaître sous son ancienne formulation dans les résultats de recherche.

**D2-T030-R04** · Erreurs corrigées et vérifiées dans la version publique | Non mesuré dans R124 | Suivi précis de chaque correctif

**D2-P0985** · Le troisième doit devenir notre indicateur prioritaire à court terme.

**D2-P0986** · Nous devons également conserver un indicateur de non-régression : une correction ne doit pas introduire de nouvelle omission, duplication, erreur de navigation ou incohérence de recherche.

**D2-P0987** · 7. Comment utiliser Codex et ClaudeCode ?

**D2-P0988** · Je recommande une répartition simple des responsabilités.

**D2-P0989** · ClaudeCode ou Codex peuvent accélérer les rapprochements de textes, la détection des duplications, la préparation des propositions de modification et l'exécution de tests reproductibles.

**D2-P0990** · L'investigation éditoriale indépendante doit déterminer si les propositions sont réellement justifiées.

**D2-P0991** · Un contrôle technique indépendant doit vérifier le candidat final, et non seulement les rapports de celui qui l'a préparé.

**D2-P0992** · Votre intervention doit se concentrer sur les décisions importantes et l'autorisation de publication.

**D2-P1050** · 2. Le problème de notre ancienne méthode

**D2-P1051** · Les investigations successives ont accompli un travail considérable.

**D2-P1052** · Nous avons retrouvé les sources, les passages, les variantes et les contextes. Nous avons également découvert des problèmes de raccordement et de duplication qui n'étaient pas apparents au départ.

**D2-P1053** · Mais notre méthode s'est progressivement transformée en programme de collation exhaustive, alors que notre priorité immédiate doit être de corriger les erreurs déjà identifiées.

**D2-P1054** · Il faut notamment éviter trois risques.

**D2-P1055** · Premier risque : continuer à découvrir de nouvelles divergences sans corriger celles qui sont déjà suffisamment documentées.

**D2-P1056** · Deuxième risque : considérer que tous les compléments doivent subir le même niveau d'examen, alors que leurs risques et leur complexité sont très différents.

**D2-P1057** · Troisième risque : préparer une version intégrale du corpus corrigé avant toute publication, ce qui retarderait inutilement les premiers bénéfices pour les utilisateurs.

**D2-P1058** · Il existe toutefois un risque inverse : corriger trop vite et introduire des doublons.

**D2-P1059** · R104 avait précisément démontré que certaines propositions de R103 pouvaient répéter du texte déjà produit par les compléments actifs.

**D2-P1060** · Nous devons donc accélérer les décisions éditoriales, sans raccourcir les vérifications techniques indispensables.

**D2-P1062** · 3. Le plan d'action que je confirme

**D2-P1063** · Je recommande une organisation en trois programmes, avec des objectifs et des critères de sortie distincts.

**D2-P1064** · PROGRAMME 1 — Corriger rapidement les erreurs importantes actuellement diffusées

**D2-P1065** · Priorité absolue.

**D2-P1066** · Nous allons constituer un premier correctif limité aux erreurs importantes, suffisamment établies et techniquement maîtrisables.

**D2-P1067** · Premier lot proposé

**D2-T033-R01** · Priorité | Passage | Décision

**D2-T033-R02** · Très élevée | T34 P004 | Arbitrer immédiatement le contresens probable

**D2-T033-R04** · Élevée | T34 P008 | Finaliser la correction du référent

**D2-T033-R05** · Élevée | T02 — 8 août 1899 | Vérifier la phrase composée avant correction

**D2-T033-R06** · Élevée | E09 — T33, 18 novembre 1934 | Vérifier le raccord et l'opposition verbale

**D2-T033-R08** · En attente | E07 | Résoudre la contradiction documentaire avant modification

**D2-P1068** · L'ordre d'examen n'est pas nécessairement l'ordre de publication.

**D2-P1070** · Si P008 et P009 sont prêts avant P004, nous devons pouvoir les corriger sans attendre.

**D2-P1071** · C'est un changement majeur par rapport à l'approche précédente.

**D2-P1072** · Ce que nous allons produire

**D2-P1073** · Pour chaque correction, il faudra un dossier très court mais complet :

**D2-P1074** · Texte actuel exact.

**D2-P1075** · Nature de l'erreur.

**D2-P1076** · Sources qui démontrent le problème.

**D2-P1077** · Texte corrigé proposé.

**D2-P1078** · Vérification de la phrase complète.

**D2-P1079** · Vérification des éventuels doublons.

**D2-P1080** · Statut éditorial : approuvé ou en attente.

**D2-P1081** · Une fois l'arbitrage éditorial effectué, les corrections seront préparées ensemble dans un correctif minimal.

**D2-P1083** · PROGRAMME 2 — Résoudre les problèmes techniques et structurels déjà identifiés

**D2-P1084** · Ce programme est complémentaire au premier.

**D2-P1085** · Les travaux antérieurs avaient signalé :

**D2-P1086** · Neuf placements historiques dont les empreintes n'étaient pas encore entièrement réconciliées.

**D2-P1087** · Quatre problèmes de bornes de locuteurs dans les données historiques.

**D2-P1088** · Des raccordements potentiellement incorrects entre le PRINCIPAL et les COMPLÉMENTS.

**D2-P1089** · Ces anomalies ne prouvent pas, à elles seules, que le lecteur de production fonctionne incorrectement.

**D2-P1090** · Mais elles constituent une liste précise de vérifications à réaliser.

**D2-P1091** · Je recommande donc de contrôler immédiatement leur comportement dans v142.19.

**D2-P1092** · Si un défaut affecte réellement le texte affiché, son ordre, sa continuité ou l'attribution des paroles, nous le traiterons comme une correction prioritaire.

**D2-P1093** · En revanche, une différence d'empreinte historique sans conséquence actuelle ne devra pas bloquer inutilement une publication.

**D2-P1094** · Le principe est simple : corriger les défauts réels, et ne pas transformer chaque anomalie documentaire en chantier technique.

**D2-P1096** · PROGRAMME 3 — Assainir progressivement l'ensemble des 75 compléments

**D2-P1097** · Ce troisième programme est important, mais il ne doit plus bloquer les deux premiers.

**D2-P1098** · Nous conserverons le registre des 75 dossiers et les recherches déjà effectuées.

**D2-P1099** · Chaque dossier sera classé selon quatre critères :

**D2-T034-R01** · Critère | Question

**D2-T034-R02** · Gravité | Le problème modifie-t-il le sens ou la compréhension du texte ?

**D2-T034-R03** · Certitude | Les sources permettent-elles réellement de conclure ?

**D2-T034-R04** · Exposition | Le défaut apparaît-il dans la lecture normale actuellement distribuée ?

**D2-T034-R05** · Complexité | La correction est-elle locale ou implique-t-elle plusieurs passages et composants ?

**D2-P1100** · Ce classement permettra d'organiser des lots de cinq à dix dossiers.

**D2-P1101** · Pour chaque dossier, nous devons aboutir à l'une des décisions suivantes : conserver le texte, le corriger, compléter un passage manquant, éliminer une répétition ou maintenir une variante non résolue.

**D2-P1102** · Une collation exhaustive restera nécessaire pour les cas véritablement complexes.

**D2-P1103** · En revanche, elle ne sera plus imposée systématiquement à chaque dossier.

**D2-P1105** · 4. Comment les corrections seront-elles réalisées techniquement ?

**D2-P1106** · C'est le point sur lequel je veux être particulièrement rigoureux.

**D2-P1107** · Une correction textuelle n'est pas nécessairement une simple modification d'un fichier JSON.

**D2-P1108** · Les différents composants de v142.19 sont liés.

**D2-P1109** · Lorsqu'un texte est modifié, nous devons examiner les dépendances suivantes :

**D2-T035-R01** · Composant | Vérification requise

**D2-T035-R02** · Corpus PRINCIPAL | Aucun changement non autorisé

**D2-T035-R03** · Compléments | Texte corrigé, identifiants et emplacement préservés

**D2-T035-R04** · Locuteurs | Découpage et positions toujours corrects

**D2-T035-R05** · Reader | Texte affiché une seule fois, au bon endroit

**D2-T035-R06** · Recherche exacte | Résultats cohérents avec le nouveau texte

**D2-T035-R07** · Recherche Par le sens | Passages et représentations correctement synchronisés

**D2-T035-R08** · Index et fichiers dérivés | Reconstruction ciblée si nécessaire

**D2-T035-R09** · Service worker | Nouvelle version correctement distribuée

**D2-T035-R10** · Mode hors ligne | Absence de maintien involontaire de textes obsolètes

**D2-T035-R11** · Données utilisateurs | Notes, favoris, surlignages et positions préservés

**D2-P1110** · Il n'est pas automatiquement nécessaire de réentraîner le modèle ONNX pour modifier quelques phrases.

**D2-P1111** · Mais il faut vérifier si les représentations sémantiques associées aux passages corrigés doivent être régénérées.

**D2-P1112** · Aucune correction ne devra être considérée comme terminée uniquement parce que le Reader affiche le nouveau texte.

**D2-P1113** · Les recherches, la navigation et les données utilisateurs doivent rester cohérentes.

**D2-P1115** · 5. L'organisation concrète du travail

**D2-P1116** · Je recommande désormais un processus avec six portes de validation.

**D2-T036-R01** · Étape | Travail | Condition pour avancer

**D2-T036-R02** · G0 | Figer la base exacte v142.19 | Empreintes et identité de distribution vérifiées

**D2-T036-R03** · G1 | Constater les problèmes dans le texte actuel | Erreurs réellement identifiées et localisées

**D2-T036-R04** · G2 | Arbitrer les corrections éditoriales | Textes avant/après validés indépendamment

**D2-T036-R05** · G3 | Préparer le correctif minimal | Modifications limitées et reproductibles

**D2-T036-R06** · G4 | Vérifier intégralement le candidat | Aucun défaut bloquant ni régression détectée

**D2-T036-R07** · G5 | Autoriser et déployer | Votre approbation explicite sur le candidat exact

**D2-P1117** · Répartition des responsabilités

**D2-P1118** · Je recommande de confier à Codex ou ClaudeCode la préparation technique des corrections, le contrôle des dépendances et l'exécution de tests reproductibles.

**D2-P1119** · Le contrôle éditorial doit être effectué indépendamment, sur les textes originaux et leurs contextes.

**D2-P1120** · Un second contrôle technique doit vérifier le candidat produit.

**D2-P1121** · Nous éviterons ainsi de faire intervenir plusieurs systèmes pour recommencer la même enquête générale.

**D2-P1122** · Votre intervention sera réservée aux approbations importantes.

**D2-P1124** · 6. Quelle version allons-nous modifier ?

**D2-P1125** · Je recommande de préparer le premier correctif à partir de v142.19, puisque c'est la version effectivement utilisée en production.

**D2-P1126** · Cela minimise les risques d'introduire des modifications non liées aux corrections éditoriales.

**D2-P1127** · Il existe toutefois un programme parallèle de développement de v142.23 sur App Test.

**D2-P1128** · Nous devons éviter que ces deux programmes divergent.

**D2-P1129** · La méthode sera donc la suivante :

**D2-P1130** · Premièrement, préparer un correctif minimal sur la base exacte de v142.19, sans modifier les fonctionnalités non concernées.

**D2-P1131** · Deuxièmement, vérifier le correctif sur App Test, avec les contrôles nécessaires.

**D2-P1132** · Troisièmement, si la version v142.23 est déjà suffisamment qualifiée au moment de la publication, examiner si une publication unique serait préférable.

**D2-P1133** · Quatrièmement, quelle que soit la version publiée, reporter les corrections éditoriales dans la future base technique afin qu'elles ne disparaissent pas lors d'une mise à jour ultérieure.

**D2-P1134** · Il faut éviter deux erreurs opposées : retarder les corrections en attendant v142.23, ou promouvoir précipitamment v142.23 alors que sa qualification n'est pas terminée.

**D2-P1135** · Par défaut, je privilégie le correctif de production minimal.

**D2-P1137** · 7. À quelle vitesse pouvons-nous avancer ?

**D2-P1138** · Je propose des objectifs de pilotage sensiblement plus courts que ceux de notre programme précédent.

**D2-T037-R03** · 1 | Finaliser les premiers arbitrages éditoriaux | Dans la même séquence de travail

**D2-T037-R04** · 2 | Préparer un premier correctif | Dès les corrections approuvées

**D2-T037-R05** · 3 | Exécuter les contrôles et préparer la publication | Sans relancer un audit général

**D2-T037-R06** · 4 | Poursuivre les autres dossiers | Lots successifs de 5 à 10

**D2-P1139** · Ce sont des objectifs de cadence, et non des engagements de calendrier : la qualification du code et la résolution des variantes peuvent prendre davantage de temps.

**D2-P1140** · Mais nous ne devons plus consacrer plusieurs itérations à simplement redémontrer qu'une omission existe.

**D2-P1141** · Lorsqu'un problème est suffisamment établi, l'étape suivante doit être sa résolution, pas un nouvel audit identique.

## Pourquoi la discordance de SHA importe

Le registre R158 n'est pas frauduleux ni totalement invalide : **son contrôle de transfert passe parce qu'il vérifie les empreintes de ses propres documents**, y compris le registre tel qu'écrit. Ce contrôle ne compare pas le SHA déclaré du `index.html` au fichier réel du delta G2. Il faut donc distinguer :

1. **Intégrité des octets archivés : PASS.**
2. **Concordance des assertions de custody internes : FAIL sur `index.html`.**
3. **Reconstruction selon le script R158 original : dangereuse pour le périmètre du correctif.**
4. **Reconstruction avec garde R159 : PASS, SHA réel rétabli.**

Le fichier historique R158 n'a **pas été réécrit**. `R159_CORRECTIF_LEDGER_ADDENDUM.json` contient l'erratum ; `R159_REPRODUCE_GUARDED_INDEX.py` reconstruit le fichier réellement testé depuis la source gelée, sans toucher à la source par défaut.
